title: Journal
description: Class 11 Accountancy: classification of accounts (personal, real, nominal and modern), the golden rules of debit and credit, recording simple and compound journal entries, and opening, closing and rectification entries.

topics.title: Classification of Accounts and the Rules of Debit and Credit
topics.concept:
A journal is the book of original entry — the first place a transaction is recorded, in date order, before it goes anywhere else. To record it we must decide which account is debited and which is credited. For that, we first classify accounts.

Traditional classification sorts every account into three types:

  • Personal accounts — of persons and firms (Ram, a bank, a company; also capital and drawings).
  • Real accounts — of assets and property (cash, building, machinery, goods).
  • Nominal accounts — of expenses, losses, incomes and gains (rent, wages, salary, commission received).

Each type has a golden rule:

TypeDebit…Credit…
Personalthe receiverthe giver
Realwhat comes inwhat goes out
Nominalall expenses & lossesall incomes & gains

The modern (accounting-equation) classification sorts accounts into Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Revenue and Expenses, and uses one consistent rule based on increase/decrease:

AccountIncreaseDecrease
AssetDebitCredit
Expense / LossDebitCredit
LiabilityCreditDebit
CapitalCreditDebit
Revenue / GainCreditDebit

Both systems give the same answer. Whichever you use, the golden test of double entry holds: for every transaction, total debits = total credits.

examples.problem: Example 1: Classify under traditional heads: (a) Cash, (b) Ram's account, (c) Rent paid.
examples.solution:
Asset / person / expense.

  • Cash → real account.
  • Ram → personal account.
  • Rent paid → nominal account.
examples.answer: Cash = real; Ram = personal; Rent paid = nominal.

examples.problem: Example 2: Using the golden rules, which account is debited when cash is paid to a creditor, Mohan?
examples.solution:
Two accounts: Mohan (personal), Cash (real).

  • Mohan receives the payment → debit the receiver (Mohan).
  • Cash goes out → credit what goes out (Cash).
examples.answer: Debit Mohan (the receiver); credit Cash (what goes out).

examples.problem: Example 3: Under the modern rule, how is an increase in an expense recorded?
examples.solution:
Expenses behave like assets.

  • An increase in an expense is a debit.
examples.answer: By a debit (increase in expense = debit).

recap:
• Journal = book of original entry. Traditional: personal (debit receiver/credit giver), real (debit comes in/credit goes out), nominal (debit expenses & losses/credit incomes & gains).
  • Modern: Asset & Expense → increase = Debit; Liability, Capital & Revenue → increase = Credit.
  • Always: total debits = total credits.

quiz.q: The golden rule for nominal accounts is: debit all expenses & losses, credit all:
quiz.explanation: Nominal: debit expenses & losses, credit incomes & gains.

quiz.q: Under the modern rule, an increase in a liability is a:
quiz.explanation: Liabilities increase on the credit side.

topics.title: Recording Journal Entries (Simple and Compound)
topics.concept:
A journal entry is written in a fixed format: the account debited first (with "Dr"), the account credited below it (prefixed "To"), a short narration in brackets, and the amounts in the debit and credit columns.

DateParticularsL.F.Dr (Rs)Cr (Rs)
 Furniture A/c   Dr 20,000 
    To Cash A/c  20,000
 (Being furniture purchased for cash)

A simple entry involves exactly two accounts (one debit, one credit). A compound entry involves more than two accounts — several debits and/or several credits in one entry, used when several things happen together. The only rule is that the total of the debit amounts must equal the total of the credit amounts.

Some standard entries to memorise:

  • Started business with cash: Cash A/c Dr, To Capital A/c.
  • Purchased goods for cash: Purchases A/c Dr, To Cash A/c.
  • Sold goods on credit to Ram: Ram A/c Dr, To Sales A/c.
  • Paid salary: Salary A/c Dr, To Cash A/c.
  • Withdrew cash for personal use: Drawings A/c Dr, To Cash A/c.

Note the difference between buying an asset (Furniture A/c) and buying goods for resale (Purchases A/c) — a very common exam trap.

examples.problem: Example 1: Journalise: Started business with cash Rs 1,00,000.
examples.solution:
Cash comes in; owner gives capital.

  • Cash A/c Dr 1,00,000 (debit what comes in).
  • To Capital A/c 1,00,000 (credit the giver).
examples.answer: Cash A/c Dr 1,00,000; To Capital A/c 1,00,000 (capital introduced).

examples.problem: Example 2: Journalise: Paid Rs 4,800 to Mohan in full settlement of Rs 5,000 (discount Rs 200).
examples.solution:
A compound entry.

  • Mohan A/c Dr 5,000 (receiver).
  • To Cash A/c 4,800 (cash out).
  • To Discount Received A/c 200 (a gain).
examples.answer: Mohan A/c Dr 5,000; To Cash A/c 4,800; To Discount Received A/c 200.

examples.problem: Example 3: Journalise: Purchased a computer for office use for cash Rs 40,000.
examples.solution:
Asset, not goods.

  • A computer for office use is an asset, not purchases.
  • Computer A/c Dr 40,000; To Cash A/c 40,000.
examples.answer: Computer A/c Dr 40,000; To Cash A/c 40,000 (it is an asset, so not 'Purchases').

recap:
• Format: debit account (Dr) first, credit account (To) below, narration in brackets, amounts in Dr/Cr columns.
  • Simple entry = two accounts; compound entry = more than two (total Dr = total Cr).
  • Goods for resale → Purchases A/c; an asset for use → the asset's own account.

quiz.q: An entry involving more than two accounts is a:
quiz.explanation: More than two accounts = a compound entry.

quiz.q: Goods purchased for resale are debited to:
quiz.explanation: Goods bought for resale are debited to Purchases A/c.

topics.title: Opening, Closing and the Idea of Rectification Entries
topics.concept:
Besides ordinary transaction entries, the journal also carries a few special entries.

  • Opening entry — passed at the start of a new year to bring forward the previous year's closing balances. All assets are debited, all liabilities and capital are credited (capital is the balancing figure). For example: Cash A/c Dr, Stock A/c Dr, Furniture A/c Dr… To Creditors A/c, To Capital A/c.
  • Closing entries — passed at the end of the year to close the nominal accounts (expenses and incomes) by transferring them to the Trading and Profit & Loss Account. For example, to close the wages account: Trading A/c Dr, To Wages A/c.
  • Adjusting entries — passed for items like outstanding expenses, prepaid expenses, depreciation, etc., so that the accounts show the correct figures for the period (studied fully in Final Accounts).
  • Rectification (rectifying) entries — passed to correct errors already made in the books. The idea: pass an entry that cancels the wrong effect and puts in the right one. A full treatment comes in the Trial Balance chapter, but the principle is introduced here: never erase an entry — correct it with another journal entry, so the trail stays honest and auditable.

So the journal is far more than a daybook of sales and purchases: it is where the year is opened, adjusted, closed and, when needed, corrected. Mastering these entry types is what turns a list of transactions into a complete, self-correcting record.

examples.problem: Example 1: In an opening entry, are assets debited or credited?
examples.solution:
Bring in balances.

  • Assets are debited; liabilities and capital are credited.
examples.answer: Assets are debited (liabilities and capital are credited).

examples.problem: Example 2: Pass the closing entry to close the Wages Account (Rs 30,000) to the Trading Account.
examples.solution:
Transfer the expense.

  • Trading A/c Dr 30,000; To Wages A/c 30,000.
examples.answer: Trading A/c Dr 30,000; To Wages A/c 30,000 (wages closed to Trading A/c).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why do we rectify an error with a fresh entry rather than erasing the wrong one?
examples.solution:
Keep the audit trail.

  • Erasing destroys evidence and looks like fraud.
  • A rectifying entry corrects the mistake while keeping a clear, honest record.
examples.answer: To keep an honest, auditable trail — the error and its correction both remain visible, unlike an erasure.

recap:
• Opening entry: brings forward balances — debit assets, credit liabilities & capital.
  • Closing entries: transfer nominal accounts to Trading/P&L at year-end.
  • Adjusting entries: outstanding/prepaid/depreciation etc. Rectifying entries: correct errors with a fresh entry (never erase).

quiz.q: An entry passed at the start of the year to bring forward balances is the:
quiz.explanation: The opening entry brings forward last year's closing balances.

quiz.q: Errors in the books should be corrected by:
quiz.explanation: Errors are corrected with a rectifying entry, never by erasing.

questions.q: The journal is the book of:
questions.explanation: The journal is the book of original (first) entry.

questions.q: Ram's account is a ____ account.
questions.explanation: Accounts of persons/firms are personal accounts.

questions.q: Cash account is a ____ account.
questions.explanation: Cash (an asset/property) is a real account.

questions.q: Rent paid is a ____ account.
questions.explanation: Expenses are nominal accounts.

questions.q: Golden rule for personal accounts:
options: Debit the receiver, credit the giver
questions.explanation: Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver.

questions.q: Golden rule for real accounts:
options: Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
questions.explanation: Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.

questions.q: Under the modern rule, an increase in an asset is a:
questions.explanation: Assets increase on the debit side.

questions.q: Under the modern rule, an increase in capital is a:
questions.explanation: Capital increases on the credit side.

questions.q: 'Started business with cash' is journalised as:
options: Cash A/c Dr, To Capital A/c
Capital A/c Dr, To Cash A/c
Purchases A/c Dr, To Cash A/c
Drawings A/c Dr, To Cash A/c
questions.explanation: Cash comes in (Dr); owner gives capital (Cr).

questions.q: An entry with more than two accounts is a:
questions.explanation: More than two accounts = compound entry.

questions.q: A machine bought for use in the factory is debited to:
questions.explanation: An asset for use is debited to its own account, not Purchases.

questions.q: Cash withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use is debited to:
questions.explanation: Owner's withdrawals are debited to Drawings A/c.

questions.q: In an opening entry, liabilities and capital are:
questions.explanation: Opening entry debits assets and credits liabilities and capital.

questions.q: Closing entries transfer nominal accounts to the:
questions.explanation: Expenses and incomes are closed to Trading and P&L.

questions.q: Errors already recorded are corrected by:
questions.explanation: A fresh rectifying entry corrects errors honestly.

questions.q: Paid Rs 9,700 to Sohan in full settlement of his account of Rs 10,000. The correct entry is:
options: Sohan A/c Dr 10,000; To Cash A/c 9,700; To Discount Received A/c 300
Cash A/c Dr 9,700; To Sohan A/c 9,700
Sohan A/c Dr 9,700; To Cash A/c 9,700
Discount A/c Dr 300; To Sohan A/c 300
questions.explanation: Sohan (receiver) is cleared for the full 10,000; cash out 9,700 and the Rs 300 saved is a discount received (gain).

questions.q: Goods costing Rs 2,000 are given away as a charity/donation. The debit goes to:
questions.explanation: Goods leaving as charity are an expense; debit Charity A/c and credit Purchases A/c.

questions.q: A student debits 'Purchases A/c' when the firm buys a delivery van for its own use. This is wrong because:
options: A van for own use is a fixed asset, not goods for resale
questions.explanation: Only goods meant for resale go to Purchases; an asset for use goes to its own account (Van A/c).

questions.q: Why do total debits always equal total credits in every journal entry?
options: Because of the dual aspect concept
questions.explanation: Each transaction has two equal aspects (dual aspect), so debits must equal credits.

questions.q: Received Rs 5,000 from Gita, allowed her Rs 100 discount. The entry is:
options: Cash A/c Dr 5,000; Discount Allowed A/c Dr 100; To Gita A/c 5,100
Gita A/c Dr 5,100; To Cash A/c 5,000
Cash A/c Dr 5,100; To Gita A/c 5,100
Discount A/c Dr 100; To Cash A/c 100
questions.explanation: Cash in 5,000 and discount allowed 100 (an expense, Dr) together clear Gita's 5,100.

questions.q: Using the modern rule, salary outstanding (unpaid) at year-end increases an expense AND creates a liability. The entry is:
options: Salary A/c Dr; To Outstanding Salary A/c
Outstanding Salary A/c Dr; To Salary A/c
Cash A/c Dr; To Salary A/c
Salary A/c Dr; To Cash A/c
questions.explanation: Expense increases (Dr Salary) and a liability is created (Cr Outstanding Salary).

questions.q: Which is a personal account in disguise?
options: Outstanding Rent A/c (a representative personal account)
questions.explanation: Outstanding/prepaid accounts represent persons, so they are representative personal accounts.

questions.q: Sold goods to Ravi for Rs 8,000 on credit. The correct entry is:
options: Ravi A/c Dr 8,000; To Sales A/c 8,000
Sales A/c Dr 8,000; To Ravi A/c 8,000
Cash A/c Dr 8,000; To Sales A/c 8,000
Ravi A/c Dr 8,000; To Cash A/c 8,000
questions.explanation: Ravi (receiver/debtor) is debited; Sales (income) is credited; no cash yet (credit sale).

questions.q: An opening entry shows assets Rs 80,000 and liabilities Rs 30,000. The capital credited will be:
questions.explanation: Capital is the balancing figure = assets − liabilities = 80,000 − 30,000 = 50,000.

questions.q: The proprietor takes goods (cost Rs 3,000) for personal use. The entry is:
options: Drawings A/c Dr 3,000; To Purchases A/c 3,000
Drawings A/c Dr 3,000; To Sales A/c 3,000
Purchases A/c Dr 3,000; To Drawings A/c 3,000
Cash A/c Dr 3,000; To Drawings A/c 3,000
questions.explanation: Goods taken for personal use are drawings; reduce purchases (goods leaving the business at cost).
